paragraphs.heading: Change across generations
paragraphs.text: Evolution is a shift, over many generations, in the inherited traits of a population of living things. It takes place when individuals differ in their genes and also differ in how many of their young survive. Biologists often put it more precisely as a change in how common particular alleles are, where an allele is one version of a gene at a given spot. Since alleles need not have any visible effect, a population can evolve even while it looks exactly the same.

paragraphs.heading: Where inherited traits live
paragraphs.text: Inherited traits pass from parents to offspring through DNA, a long molecule built from four kinds of bases. The order of those bases carries the information, much as the order of letters spells out a sentence. A stretch of DNA that sets up one working unit is a gene, and the full set of an organism's genes is its genotype. The traits you can actually observe, in body and behaviour, make up its phenotype.

paragraphs.heading: Not every trait is inherited
paragraphs.text: A phenotype comes from both the genotype and the surroundings an organism has lived in. A suntan is a good example: it arises when a person's genes meet sunlight, so it is not handed down to that person's children. The phenotype in this case is the skin's ability to tan when sunlight falls on it. People differ in how easily they tan, and those with albinism, an inherited trait, do not tan at all.

paragraphs.heading: The raw material of change
paragraphs.text: Evolution needs genetic variation within a population. New variation appears through mutations, which change DNA and create new alleles. Sexual reproduction shuffles existing genes, and migration between populations, called gene flow, moves them around. Even so, most of a species' genome is very similar from one individual to the next.

paragraphs.heading: What makes variants spread
paragraphs.text: Once variation exists, several processes make some alleles more common and others rarer over time. These are natural selection, genetic drift and gene flow, with mutation supplying the new material. Generation after generation, the offspring of parents with traits that suit their surroundings tend to take the place of other members of the population.

paragraphs.heading: Darwin, Wallace and after
paragraphs.text: Charles Darwin and Alfred Russel Wallace, two British naturalists, each arrived at the idea of evolution by natural selection in the mid-19th century. They were trying to explain why living things fit their surroundings so well. Darwin laid the theory out in detail in On the Origin of Species. In the early 20th century, evolution was joined with Mendelian inheritance and population genetics, and that union became modern evolutionary theory.

paragraphs.heading: One family tree for all life
paragraphs.text: Every living thing on Earth, people included, descends from a last universal common ancestor that lived roughly 3.5–3.8 billion years ago. Today's variety of life was shaped by new species forming, species changing, and species dying out. Species with a more recent shared ancestor tend to look and work more alike. Biologists once used such likenesses to build family trees, but now they mostly compare genetic sequences directly.
